lena.name: Dr. Lena Reyes
lena.role: field biologist (a scientist who studies animals in the wild)

case.title: The One-Year Jump
case.hook: After the big oak, I wanted to know how scientists check a whole ecosystem. So I flew! Every winter, scientists ride in small planes over Florida’s springs and rivers and count every manatee they can see. Look at two of the state’s flight logs. In one year, the count jumped by 1,275 manatees.

logs.head: Flight log · statewide
logs.alt: Dozens of manatees resting close together in a clear Florida spring.

logs.head: Flight log · statewide
logs.alt: Seen from an airplane: a huge group of gray manatees packed together in a blue-green spring.

case.sticky: 1,275 more manatees in ONE year? Is that real?
case.stillsCredit: Counts: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) synoptic aerial surveys. Photos (public domain): manatees at Three Sisters Springs, Steve Hillebrand, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service; manatees from the air at Crystal River National Wildlife Refuge, U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service.
case.question: Did Florida really gain 1,275 manatees in one year, and how can scientists tell if a Florida ecosystem is healthy?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.where: Warm-Up: count it or feel it?
clues.t: Scientists trust things they can count or measure, not feelings.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 2: fly the survey
clues.t: A count depends on the weather. Cold, calm days pack manatees into warm springs, where they are easy to see. The same manatees can give very different counts.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 3: four Florida stories
clues.t: Numbers measured over many years show which places are recovering (manatees, wood storks) and which are out of balance (pythons, lionfish).

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: thirty years of counts
clues.t: One year can fool you. Counts bounce up and down, but over 30 years they climbed a lot, and scientists now estimate 8,350 to 11,730 manatees.

solve.title: Did the manatees really jump?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Yes. 1,275 new manatees appeared in one year.
options.why: Check Clue 2. The weather can change a count a lot, even when the number of manatees stays the same.

options.t: One count can’t prove it. Weather changes counts, but 30 years of data show manatees really have recovered. Scientists keep measuring to catch new problems.
options.why: Case cracked! A jump in one year can come partly from the weather. Many years of measurements are what show the real story. Now write your case report: it’s the questions below.

options.t: Counts are useless, so nobody can know.
options.why: Check Clues 3 and 4. Many years of careful measurements do tell a real story.

judge.title: Count it or feel it?
todo: Read the card about the two wetlands.
Drag it to a side, or tap a side.
Ask: could a scientist write down a number for this?

why.t: Two people can feel differently about the same place. A number someone measured stays the same no matter who reads it.

judge.hint: Read the card, then drag it to a side, or tap a side.

cards.t: We counted 42 wading birds in one hour.
cards.why: A count is a number anyone can check.
Peaceful is a feeling. Someone else might feel bored or scared.
cards.miss: Can you write down a number for “peaceful”?

cards.t: We found 11 different kinds of fish.
cards.why: Counting the kinds of living things is a big clue to health. More kinds usually means more balance.

cards.t: The water looks kind of gross.
cards.why: Gross is a feeling. A scientist would measure how clear the water is instead.
cards.miss: Is “gross” a number? What could you measure instead?

cards.t: We could see the bottom 6 feet down.
cards.why: How far you can see is a measurement of how clear the water is.

cards.t: It seems like there are fewer frogs this year.
cards.why: “It seems” is a guess. Counting frogs every year would turn it into evidence.
cards.miss: Did anyone count the frogs? “It seems” is a clue.

cards.t: Hunters removed 3 pythons from this wetland this year.
cards.why: That’s a count someone wrote down.

cards.t: I just have a good feeling about this place.
cards.why: A good feeling isn’t evidence. Numbers are.

judge.win: All 8 sorted! That’s Clue 1: scientists trust what they can count or measure. Now answer the warm-up question below.

survey.afterText: the data is the only way to spot it
survey.title: Fly the survey
todo: Pick the weather and the wind.
Press Fly the survey and watch the count.
Fly at least 3 times with different weather. Then answer the question.

why.t: Manatees spread out across rivers and bays, so scientists count them from small planes flying low over the water. When water gets cold, manatees crowd into warm springs to stay warm.

survey.alt: Seen from an airplane: a huge group of gray manatees packed together in a blue-green spring.
survey.credit: Manatees gathered at a warm spring, Crystal River National Wildlife Refuge, Florida. U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, public domain.
survey.note: This is a model (a practice version). On every flight, the same 200 manatees live near this spring.
survey.bestHint: Try one more flight: which weather would pack the most manatees into the spring, where you can see them best?

q.q: The same 200 manatees lived here on every flight. Why did your counts change?

opts.t: Manatees were born and died between flights.
opts.why: The model kept the same 200 manatees every time. What changed was the weather.

opts.t: Cold weather packs them into the warm spring, and calm water makes them easier to see.
opts.why: Right! That’s Clue 2. A count can change with the weather even when the number of manatees doesn’t.

opts.t: The plane flew faster on some days.
opts.why: Look at what you changed: the weather and the wind.

verdict.title: Four Florida stories: recovering or out of balance?
todo: Tap a story to open its data.
Stamp it: Recovering or Out of balance.
Then pick the line that proves it. Do all four.

why.t: Proof is a number someone measured, usually over many years. A feeling or a fun fact is not proof.

verdict.credit: Photos (public domain): manatee, Keith Ramos, USFWS; Burmese python in the Everglades, Bryan Falk, USGS; red lionfish, Paula Whitfield, NOAA (photographed off North Carolina; the same kind lives on Florida reefs); wood stork, National Park Service.

stories.name: Florida manatees
stories.alt: A manatee swimming over sand with a school of small fish.
data: 1991: scientists counted about 1,200 manatees from airplanes.
2017: the government moved manatees from “endangered” to “threatened” because their numbers rose.

proof.t: Counts and estimates rose a lot over about 30 years.
Manatees look happy in the springs.
proof.miss: Happy is a feeling. Which line has numbers?
True, but it doesn’t show whether they are recovering.

stories.why: Speed limits for boats, protected springs and rescues helped. Scientists still watch closely: in 2021, more than 1,000 manatees died, most from hunger after seagrass died in a polluted lagoon.

stories.name: Burmese pythons
stories.alt: A large Burmese python with brown and tan patches coiled in grass.
data: Pythons don’t belong in Florida. Many were pets that escaped or were let go.
In parts of the Everglades with many pythons, scientists counted about 99 out of every 100 raccoons and opossums gone, compared with years before.

proof.t: Raccoons and opossums dropped about 99% where pythons live.

proof.miss: Scary is a feeling. Which line has a number?
True, but it doesn’t show what they did to the ecosystem.

stories.why: An invasive species (one that doesn’t belong and causes harm) with no natural enemies here can wipe out native animals.

stories.name: Lionfish
stories.alt: A striped lionfish with long spiky fins swimming over a reef.
data: Lionfish come from the Pacific and Indian Oceans. They don’t belong in Florida.
In one study, a single lionfish ate 20 small fish in 30 minutes.
Divers now hold special hunts to remove them.

proof.t: One lionfish ate 20 small fish in 30 minutes.

proof.miss: Beautiful is a feeling. Which line has numbers?
True, but it doesn’t show harm to the reef.

stories.why: Native reef fish didn’t evolve to escape lionfish, so lionfish can eat many of them fast.

stories.name: Everglades wood storks
stories.alt: A tall white wood stork with a dark, bare head and a long thick beak, standing in tall grass.
data: People drained much of the Everglades, and wading birds like wood storks lost places to feed and nest.
Florida and the U.S. are putting water back in the Everglades.
2014: wood storks moved from “endangered” to “threatened” as their numbers grew.

proof.t: Wood storks moved from “endangered” to “threatened” as their numbers grew.
Everglades restoration costs a lot of money.
proof.miss: Money spent isn’t proof the birds are doing better.
True, but it says nothing about recovery.

stories.why: Recovery takes decades, and scientists keep counting nests to be sure it lasts.

verdict.win: All four decided! That’s Clue 3: numbers measured over years show which places are recovering and which are out of balance.

trend.afterText: Every dot on the chart below is one real survey flight
trend.title: One year, or thirty?
todo: Look at two flights, one year apart. Did the count go up or down?
Answer the question about all 30 years.

why.t: Scientists have flown these surveys most winters since 1991. One dot can mislead you; lots of dots show the real pattern.

trend.alt: Dot chart of Florida manatee airplane counts from 1991 to 2019, rising from about 1,300 to about 6,000, with estimate bars for 2016 and 2022.
trend.pairText: Here are two flights, one year apart: January 2010 and January 2011. Did the count go up or down?
trend.pairWin: Down by {diff}! If you only saw these two flights, you might worry the manatees were in trouble. But is that the whole story?
trend.allText: Every dot is one airplane count. The dashed line shows the overall direction. The green bars are newer estimates of all the manatees in Florida, including ones the planes miss.

q.q: What do 30 years of data show?

opts.t: Manatees have been going down since 2010.
opts.why: That was one dip. Look at the dashed line and the green bars after 2010.

opts.t: Counts bounce up and down, but over 30 years they climbed a lot.
opts.why: Yes! That’s Clue 4. Ups and downs happen from year to year, but the long pattern shows a real recovery.

opts.t: Each count is the exact number of manatees in Florida.
opts.why: Planes always miss some manatees. That’s why scientists also make estimates (the green bars).

trend.win: Even so, 2021 was a hard year: more than 1,000 manatees died, most from hunger after seagrass died.

q1.A: Pythons were brought here from far away. Do they belong in Florida?
q1.C: A pollinator carries pollen. Pythons eat animals.

q2.A: One photo shows one moment. What tells a longer story?
q2.B: A feeling isn’t a measurement. Which choice has numbers?

q3.B: Manatees have always lived in Florida. Invasive means they don’t belong.
q3.C: Growing numbers show protection is working. What might happen if it stopped?

welcome.label: Welcome · the flight logs
welcome.script: Welcome back! After the big oak, I had a new question: how do scientists check if a whole ecosystem is healthy? So I flew. Every winter, scientists count manatees from small planes. Look at these two flight logs. In just one year, the count jumped by more than twelve hundred. Did that many manatees really show up? Let’s find out.

warmup.label: Warm-Up · count it or feel it
warmup.script: Here’s a field secret. Two scientists can stand in the same wetland and feel totally different about it. That’s why we don’t trust feelings. We trust numbers. Read each card and decide: could a scientist measure this, or is it just a feeling?

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Say each word; act out balance on one foot.

part2.label: Part 2 · fly the survey (Clue 2)
part2.script: Buckle up. This is a practice survey flight. The same two hundred manatees live near this spring every day. Pick the weather, pick the wind, and fly. Then change one thing and fly again. Watch your count closely. I learned something about my own flight logs this way.

part3.label: Part 3 · four Florida stories (Clue 3)
part3.script: Some Florida stories are getting better, and some are in trouble. Open each case file and read the data. Stamp it, then find the line that really proves it. Careful: some lines are true but don’t prove anything.

explore.label: Part 4 · thirty years of counts (Clue 4)
explore.script: Every dot on this chart is one real flight. Start with just two of them, one year apart. Then show them all. This is my favorite chart in Florida, because it taught me not to panic over one bad year.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: You have all four clues. Crack the case at the top of this tab first: did the manatees really jump by twelve hundred in one year? Then write your report. Build your own manatee graph in Part C, and use real numbers as your evidence. Your answers save as you type.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: Some people say invasive species are no big deal, because Florida has plenty of native animals. Hmm. Think about the python and lionfish files you opened. Pick your side, choose two pieces of evidence in the planner, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.notes: Celebrate; tease 11.01 (body parts built for survival).
closing.script: Case closed, field scientist. One count can fool you, but many years of numbers tell the truth. Next week, we zoom in on the living things themselves: the body parts that help Florida plants and animals survive. See you in the field.

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me tell if an ecosystem is healthy, or what people can do?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: In 1991, scientists in airplanes counted about 1,200 manatees in Florida.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “1991”, “counted” and “1,200 manatees”. Those words tell when, how and how many. Small words like “in” and “about” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.

tool.name: Secchi disk
tool.teaser: A black-and-white disk on a rope: how scientists measure how clear the water is.
tool.done: You tested three Florida waters with a Secchi disk and found out why clear water matters for seagrass and manatees. A Secchi disk sticker is in your Field Notebook.

why.q: Why a Secchi disk this week?
why.t: Clear water lets sunlight reach seagrass, and seagrass is manatee food. A Secchi disk (say it: SECK-ee) is a simple tool that measures how clear water is, so it’s one number scientists and volunteers use to check a lake or lagoon’s health.

secchi.title: How clear is the water?
todo: Tap each part of the disk to learn it.
Pick a place, then lower the disk one foot at a time.
Press “I can’t see it anymore!” the moment it disappears. Test all three places.

parts.label: The disk
parts.t: A flat disk about as wide as a dinner plate, painted in black and white parts so your eye can tell when it fades away.

parts.label: The rope
parts.t: Marked every foot, so you can read how deep the disk is when it disappears.

parts.label: The weight
parts.t: Hangs under the disk so it sinks straight down instead of floating sideways.

sites.name: A clear Florida spring
sites.note: You can still see the disk on the bottom! Spring water is so clear that the disk never disappears here.

sites.name: A lagoon on a normal day
sites.note: About 4 feet. Sunlight still reaches seagrass in the shallow parts.

sites.name: The same lagoon in an algae bloom
sites.note: Only about 1 foot! Tiny algae turn the water green and block the sunlight.

q.q: In 2021, more than 1,000 manatees died, most from hunger. Which reading helps explain why?

opts.why: Clear springs are good for seagrass. Which reading shows sunlight being blocked?
Yes! In blooms, the water got so murky that sunlight couldn’t reach the seagrass. The seagrass died, and the manatees that eat it went hungry.
Look at the bloom reading again. What happens to plants on the bottom when sunlight can’t reach them?
